title: U.S. Loses Its Measles Elimination Status, a Historic Setback for American Health
summary: The nation was once regarded as a global leader for reining in the highly contagious virus. Now, large outbreaks that sicken thousands could become routine.

Measles has come roaring back in the United States, as vaccination rates have fallen and cases of the once-extinguished virus have soared. That backslide has now cost the nation its measles elimination status, after the virus spread uninterrupted for more than a year.


“It’s a giant stain on our reputation,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “Everyone ought to be just utterly disgusted by the willing return back to an age of death and high cost.”


The announcement, made Tuesday by the Pan American Health Organization, ushers in a new era in which major outbreaks could routinely disrupt communities around the nation, sickening thousands of children. It also marks a highly embarrassing reversal for a country that showed the rest of the world it was possible to rein in the wildly contagious virus when it[won elimination status in 2000](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/well/us-measles-elimination.html) .


State health officials have reported more than 7,700 cases of measles, including 10 deaths, since the resurgence first kicked off in a Mennonite community in Texas in January 2025. Hundreds have been hospitalized, many of them unvaccinated children. **** Infections have also risen among[pregnant women and newborns](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/well/measles-pregnancy-newborns.html) , who are at increased risk of death and other dire health consequences.


“Losing measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of the Pan American Health Organization, in a news conference announcing the decision. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at the risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death.”


The organization also announced on Tuesday that Bolivia and Mexico had also lost its measles elimination status, posing another setback for North America’s handle on the highly contagious virus. Canada officially[lost its measles elimination status](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/10/world/canada/canada-measles-what-to-know.html) last year.
